newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-News sees Ansett profit this year.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-News sees Ansett profit this year.

text.p: News Corp Ltd is optimistic that airline Ansett Australia will return to profitability in the current year to June 30, 1997, News Ltd and Ansett executive chairman Ken Cowley said on Tuesday.
He also said News, which owns 50 percent of Ansett, had no plans at the moment to float off Ansett.
Earlier Cowley and Air New Zealand Ltd chief executive Jim McCrea formally announced the conclusion of Air New Zealand's purchase of TNT Ltd's 50 percent stake in Ansett.
"Before Air New Zealand came on board, it was always the intention and determination of the Ansett team to return the company to profit this year," Cowley told the news conference.
"That is still the intention," he said adding that the partnership with Air New Zealand improved the prospects for profitability.
"I'm quite optimistic about making profits this year."
The terms of the deal were announced earlier this month, with Air New Zealand paying TNT A$325 million and agreeing to invest a further A$150 million in Ansett.
News also agreed to invest A$50 million in Ansett to help fund the rejuvenation of its fleet, which has struggled to compete with Qantas' newer and bigger planes.
Ansett made a pre-tax and pre-abnormals loss in the year to June 30, 1996.
Air New Zealand's McCrea said his earlier comments in May about a possible float of Ansett at some stage were premature.
"I think I had a rush of blood to the head when I said that a while back," McCrea said.
"I don't have a clear view on how that might go," he said.
"Both shareholders are committed to Ansett and to see that we add value in it."
Cowley said News was committed to Ansett.
"There are no considerations at the moment about floating off Ansett," he said.
"If we did it down the road a bit, it would be on the basis that it was in the best interest of Ansett, whether it was for equity reasons or for financial reasons," Cowley said.
"But there's no plans at the moment."
Seperately, McCrea said Air New Zealand had no plans to close down its budget airline, Freedom Air, which was set up in late 1995 to compete against privately-held Kiwi International Airlines Ltd.
Kiwi collapsed last month.
"Freedom will certainly be there as long as the market is there and we're endeavouring to develop that market, to sustain that sort of operation," he said.
"But you do have to see some flexibility in some of these products." -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
